title: The United Nations and Non-Alignment
tagline: The organisation built to keep the peace, and the movement of states that refused to join the Cold War blocs.

overview.intro: The United Nations was created in 1945 to do what the League of Nations had failed to do, and it was joined within fifteen years by a second body of ideas — the Non-Aligned Movement, which asserted that the newly independent states of Asia and Africa need not choose between the two armed blocs that divided the world. This chapter sets out the formation of the United Nations, its principal organs and agencies, and its record of achievements and failures, and then turns to non-alignment, its origins in Bandung and Panchsheel, its principles and leaders, and its role during the Cold War. The examination pattern is consistent: organs and agencies are marked by name and function, while non-alignment is a question of principles, leaders and evaluation.

learn.title: The formation and aims of the United Nations

blocks.text: The United Nations was built in stages while the war was still being fought. The Declaration by United Nations, signed at Washington on 1 January 1942 by twenty-six nations including the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and China, first used the name and pledged to use their full resources against the Axis. The Declaration of Moscow of 1943 recognised the need for an international organisation, and the Dumbarton Oaks conference of 1944, held by the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and China, drafted the basic plan with a Security Council at its centre. The San Francisco Conference of April to June 1945, attended by fifty-one nations, signed the Charter on 26 June 1945, and the Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, which is celebrated as United Nations Day. The aims set out in the Charter are to maintain international peace and security, to develop friendly relations among nations on the principle of equal rights and self-determination, to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social and cultural problems and in promoting respect for human rights, and to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations. The organisation is built on the sovereign equality of its members, on the obligation to settle disputes peacefully, and on the promise not to resort to force against any other state except in self-defence or as the Security Council directs.

items: Declaration by United Nations, 1 January 1942: twenty-six nations first used the name and pledged their resources against the Axis.
The Declaration of Moscow, 1943 recognised the need for a permanent international organisation.
Dumbarton Oaks, 1944 produced the basic draft with a Security Council empowered to act.
The San Francisco Conference of 1945, with fifty-one nations, signed the Charter on 26 June 1945.
The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, celebrated as United Nations Day.
Aims: peace and security, friendly relations and self-determination, cooperation on economic and social questions, and human rights.

learn.title: The principal organs of the United Nations

blocks.text: The Charter establishes six principal organs, and a full answer names each with its composition and function. The General Assembly is the parliament of the world: all members are represented, each with one vote, it discusses any question within the Charter, makes recommendations, and controls the budget and the election of the non-permanent members of the Security Council. The Security Council has primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security, consists of fifteen members of whom five are permanent — Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States — each holding a veto, and the remaining ten are elected for two-year terms; it can investigate disputes, call on parties to settle peacefully, impose sanctions and authorise the use of force. The Economic and Social Council coordinates the work of the specialised agencies and promotes economic and social progress and human rights. The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague, is composed of fifteen judges elected for nine years, and settles disputes between states that accept its jurisdiction and gives advisory opinions. The Trusteeship Council oversaw the administration of trust territories until they became self-governing. The Secretariat, headed by the Secretary-General, carries out the day-to-day work, prepares studies and reports, and services the other organs, and its staff owe their duty to the organisation alone.

items: General Assembly: all members, one vote each, discussion of any question, recommendations, and control of the budget.
Security Council: fifteen members with five permanent members holding the veto; primary responsibility for peace and security.
Economic and Social Council: coordination of the agencies and promotion of economic, social and human rights work.
International Court of Justice: fifteen judges at The Hague settling disputes between states and giving advisory opinions.
Trusteeship Council: supervised trust territories until self-government; now effectively completed its work.
Secretariat: the Secretary-General and staff carrying out the work of the organisation and serving it independently.

learn.title: The agencies of the United Nations and its record

blocks.text: Around the organs stands the wider system of agencies, each with a field of its own. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, founded in 1945, works for peace through education, science and culture, campaigns against illiteracy and defends cultural heritage. The World Health Organization, founded in 1948, directs international health work, coordinates the eradication of diseases and sets standards, and is credited with the eradication of smallpox. UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund, cares for children’s health, nutrition and education, especially in emergencies. The International Labour Organization, which predates the United Nations and was absorbed into its system, works for fair labour standards, and the Food and Agriculture Organization fights hunger and improves agriculture. The record of the United Nations is mixed. Its achievements include the settlement of several disputes by mediation and observation, the decolonisation of trust territories, humanitarian and health programmes reaching millions, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 and the development of international law. Its failures include the inability to prevent the major wars and conflicts of the Cold War era, the paralysis of the Security Council whenever a permanent member was involved, and the gap between resolutions and enforcement. The balanced judgement is that the United Nations has kept dialogue alive where the League collapsed into silence, but it can act only as far as its most powerful members allow.

items: UNESCO, founded 1945: education, science and culture, including the campaign against illiteracy.
WHO, founded 1948: international health direction and the eradication of smallpox.
UNICEF: children’s health, nutrition and education, especially in emergencies.
ILO and FAO: fair labour standards and the fight against hunger within the United Nations system.
Achievements: peacekeeping and observation missions, decolonisation, humanitarian programmes, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the growth of international law.
Failures: inability to prevent major wars, Security Council paralysis when a great power is involved, and weak enforcement of resolutions.

learn.title: The Non-Aligned Movement: origins, principles and leaders

blocks.text: Non-alignment grew out of the situation of the newly independent states after 1945. Caught between two armed blocs whose rivalry took the form of alliances, military bases and nuclear arsenals, the states of Asia and Africa found that alignment meant being drawn into conflicts that were not theirs, and that the great powers competed for their support rather than for their welfare. The ideas were first set out by Jawaharlal Nehru, whose foreign policy rested on Panchsheel — the five principles of peaceful coexistence adopted in the Sino-Indian agreement of 1954: mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. The Bandung Conference of 1955, meeting in Indonesia with Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno, Zhou Enlai and others, carried the ideas forward and issued a call for peace, cooperation and an end to colonialism, and the movement was formally launched at Belgrade in 1961 by President Tito of Yugoslavia, with Nehru of India, Nasser of Egypt, Sukarno of Indonesia and Nkrumah of Ghana among its principal founders. Its principles are respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality, peaceful settlement of disputes and no participation in military alliances. Its contribution was to give the small and newly independent states an independent voice, to keep them out of the bloc rivalry, to support decolonisation and to press for peaceful settlement in Korea, the Congo and the Middle East, though critics pointed out that non-alignment sometimes meant little more than equal distance, and that members often relied on one bloc or the other for arms and aid.

items: Origins: the independence of dozens of Asian and African states after 1945 and the pressure to join one of the two blocs.
Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence, adopted in 1954, supplied the doctrine.
The Bandung Conference of 1955 brought Asian and African leaders together and issued the call for peace and cooperation.
The Belgrade summit of 1961 formally launched the Non-Aligned Movement under Tito, with Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah as founders.
Principles: sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality, peaceful settlement and no military alliances.
Contribution: an independent voice for new states, support for decolonisation and mediation in regional conflicts; criticised for inconsistency between principle and practice.

No interference in each other’s internal affairs

items.note: The Asian-African conference that turned individual neutralisms into a collective voice, and whose final declaration called for respect for sovereignty and an end to colonialism.
The movement proposed and pressed for peaceful settlement in conflicts such as the Congo and the Suez crisis, acting as an intermediary between the blocs.

The five principles of peaceful coexistence adopted in 1954 which became the basis of non-aligned policy.

The state of rivalry without direct war between the United States-led and Soviet-led blocs, from which non-alignment sought to stand apart.

learn.title: Evaluating the United Nations and non-alignment

blocks.text: Both subjects end with an evaluation, and both are best handled by naming what was achieved, what failed and why. The United Nations achieved more than the League: it kept a forum of all states in permanent session, supervised the independence of trust territories, organised health and food programmes that reached hundreds of millions, established the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and developed international law, and its peacekeeping and observation missions helped end several regional conflicts. Its failures were structural: the veto gave five powers the ability to block action in their own interest, the great power rivalry of the Cold War paralysed the Council on the central questions, and enforcement depended on members who were unwilling to supply troops or to be bound. Non-alignment achieved a great deal for a movement with no army and no treasury: it gave the new states a voice independent of the blocs, kept several of them out of wars that were not theirs, supported decolonisation in Africa and Asia and pressed for peaceful settlement, and it gave the world a third position when the choice seemed to be between two. Its weaknesses were the inconsistency between the principle of judgement on merit and the practice of leaning on one bloc for arms and aid, the differences among its members over specific conflicts, and the influence of domestic politics on what was presented as principle. The fair conclusion is that both institutions worked within limits set by the power of the great states, and both kept open the possibility of negotiation that would otherwise have closed.

items: United Nations achievements: a permanent forum, decolonisation, health and food programmes, human rights standards and international law.
United Nations failures: the veto, Cold War paralysis and the absence of enforcement power.
Non-alignment achievements: an independent voice, freedom from bloc wars, support for decolonisation and mediation in conflicts.
Non-alignment weaknesses: inconsistency between principle and practice, internal divisions and dependence on the blocs for arms and aid.
Common limit: both were constrained by the power of the great states that dominated the post-war order.
Common value: both kept open a channel of negotiation when the alternative was confrontation.

questions.prompt: State the principles of the Non-Aligned Movement.
questions.answer: The principles are respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states, non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and refusal to participate in military alliances. Non-aligned states undertake to judge each international question on its merits rather than in the interest of a bloc, and to cooperate with all states on the basis of Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence adopted in 1954.

questions.prompt: Describe the formation of the United Nations and state its principal aims.
questions.answer: The United Nations was built in stages during the Second World War. The Declaration by United Nations, signed at Washington on 1 January 1942 by twenty-six nations, first used the name and pledged their full resources against the Axis powers. The Declaration of Moscow of 1943 recognised the need for a permanent international organisation, and the Dumbarton Oaks conference of 1944, attended by the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and China, drafted the basic plan with a Security Council at its centre. The San Francisco Conference of April to June 1945, attended by fifty-one nations, signed the Charter on 26 June 1945, and the Charter came into force on 24 October 1945. The aims set out in the Charter are to maintain international peace and security, to develop friendly relations among nations on the basis of equal rights and self-determination, to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social and cultural problems and in promoting respect for human rights, and to serve as a centre for harmonising the actions of nations. The organisation rests on the sovereign equality of its members, the obligation to settle disputes peacefully and the undertaking not to resort to force against any other state.

questions.prompt: Assess the achievements and failures of the United Nations in maintaining peace and promoting human welfare.
questions.answer: Achievements: the United Nations kept a permanent forum of all states in being, where the League had allowed disputes to drift into war, and it settled or helped to settle a number of disputes through mediation, observation missions and good offices. Through the Trusteeship Council and the work of the Assembly it oversaw the independence of trust territories and supported decolonisation, so that the number of member states grew from fifty-one to nearly two hundred. Its agencies — WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF, the FAO and the ILO — carried out health, education, nutrition and labour programmes reaching hundreds of millions, and smallpox was eradicated under WHO direction. In law and morals it produced the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 and contributed to the development of international law and the law of the sea. Failures: the veto allowed any of the five permanent members to block action in its own interest, so the Security Council was paralysed during the Cold War on the questions that mattered most; the United Nations could not prevent the major wars and many regional conflicts; and its resolutions often went unenforced because members would not supply forces or accept binding decisions. The balanced verdict is that the United Nations has been effective where the great powers permitted agreement, and that its record is the measure of their agreement rather than of its own powers.
questions.explanation: Three achievements with named examples, three failures with the structural reason, and a verdict on the constraint of the great powers.

questions.prompt: Trace the growth of the Non-Aligned Movement and evaluate its contribution to world peace.
questions.answer: The movement grew out of the position of the newly independent states of Asia and Africa after 1945, which found themselves pressed to join one of the two armed blocs while their own needs were reconstruction and development. The doctrine was first set out by Jawaharlal Nehru, whose policy rested on Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence adopted in the Sino-Indian agreement of 1954. The Bandung Conference of 1955 brought together Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno, Zhou Enlai and others and issued a call for peace, cooperation and an end to colonialism, and the movement was formally launched at the Belgrade summit of 1961 by Tito with Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah among its founders. Its contribution to peace was substantial for a movement with no army and no treasury: it gave the small and new states an independent voice, kept several of them out of wars that were not their own, supported decolonisation, and pressed for peaceful settlement in the Congo, the Middle East and the Suez crisis, acting as a channel of communication between the blocs at moments when they had ceased to speak to one another. Its weaknesses were the inconsistency between the principle of judging each question on merit and the practice of leaning on one bloc for arms and aid, the divisions among members over particular conflicts, and the influence of domestic politics on what was claimed as principle. The fair conclusion is that non-alignment did not end the Cold War, but it prevented the Cold War from absorbing the whole of Asia and Africa into itself.
questions.explanation: Origins, Panchsheel, Bandung and Belgrade, then achievements, weaknesses and a conclusion on its place in the Cold War.
